result.summary: Aristomenes proves he is alive by destroying a Corinthian relief force at night and offering the Hecatomphonia sacrifice again. During a truce, Cretan mercenaries capture him, but a Messenian girl, guided by a dream, makes them drunk and frees him, and he kills them. Her reward is marriage to his son Gorgus.

scenes.title: Night attack on the Corinthians
scenes.summary: Spartans doubt that Aristomenes has returned until he slaughters a careless Corinthian camp near Eira. He sacrifices the Hecatomphonia to Zeus of Ithome.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians' last stronghold at Eira is threatened by Spartan allies; Aristomenes risks defeat by a larger force.

scenes.title: Aristomenes captured in the truce
scenes.summary: During a festival truce, Cretan bowmen ambush and bind Aristomenes. Two go to Sparta while five take him to a farm.
scenes.stakes: Aristomenes faces imprisonment and death at Spartan hands.

scenes.title: The maiden's dream and rescue
scenes.summary: A girl who dreamed of a lion freed from wolves recognises Aristomenes, gets the Cretans drunk and frees him. He kills them, and his son Gorgus marries her.
scenes.stakes: Aristomenes' life; the girl risks death for helping an enemy captive.

notable_quotes.reason: The maiden's dream of a freed lion tearing wolves apart foretells the rescue.

analysis.text: Aristomenes is presented as a near-legendary hero whose cunning and luck, aided by dreams and ordinary people, repeatedly rescue him.
The Hecatomphonia, a sacrifice for killing a hundred enemies, and the truce for the Hyacinthia show how religion shaped warfare in the Messenian Wars.

fun_facts.text: Cretan archers were famous mercenaries in the Greek world, which explains their hire here.

language_notes.text: "Lacedæmonians" is the usual name for the Spartans, after their region Laconia (Lacedaemon).
Hecatomphonia means roughly "slaughter of a hundred," a sacrifice offered by a warrior who had killed a hundred enemies.
Refers to an earlier battle of Aristomenes against the Spartans, at the place called Boar's Memorial, described earlier in Pausanias' account.
"Bands of their quivers" means the straps or cords used to carry the quivers, which the Cretans used as ropes.
"Fatherless maiden" means an unmarried girl whose father was dead.
"Requited" means repaid; the marriage is presented as repayment for her saving his life.

context_notes.text: Corinth was an ally of Sparta in this Messenian war. Eira was the mountain stronghold where Aristomenes and the Messenians made their last stand.
The Hyacinthia was a major Spartan festival honouring Hyacinthus and Apollo. Sparta customarily observed a truce during it.
Cretan archers were famous and often hired as mercenaries in Greek armies.

literary_notes.text: Comparing Aristomenes' return to a dead man living again shows how formidable and almost supernatural his reputation was.
Aristomenes is captured because he feels secure during the truce. His trust in the truce leads to his capture.
The lion stands for Aristomenes and the wolves for his captors. The dream foretells his rescue and revenge.
The girl's recognition of the dream's meaning signals that she will free him.
